utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

I would like to ask the Prosecution to provide us with a list of those documents without English translations as soon as possible so that we can make a finding on that. I think we have to revert these documents into marked for identification pending translation. Hopefully that will not happen again. Of course, not pursuant 92 bis decision in the whole but with the specific witness. If there is nothing else to raise, the witness, the next witness, should be brought in. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and happy new years to you, Your Honours, to the Defence and everyone. Just while the witness is being brought in, Mr. President, I just want to know that this witness will require a Rule 90 caution as was given in the last trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Thayer for the Prosecution will examine you in a moment, but before he starts, on his request I would like to give a caution to you. We have rules -- a rule in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, this is Rule 90(E) which has to do with your personal situation in court, and I would like to read it out to you so that you are aware of your situation. It reads as follows: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent Prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Sir, did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Thayer is commencing his examination-in-chief. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Milorad Bircakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The exhibits in the list beginning with 65 ter 00362 through 65 ter 003391 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these documents shall be assigned exhibit numbers in the range from P1747 to P1752. And one other remark, 65 ter document 00213 has already been admitted into evidence as P18. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This number is mentioned in the list already, in the list of the Prosecution. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll proceed with the 92 ter summary. The witness was a member of the Zvornik Brigade's military police company based at the brigade command in the Standard factory in Karakaj. In July 1995, the witness served as the driver for the brigade's chief of security, Drago Nikolic. In the morning of 14 July 1995, the brigade's deputy chief of security, Milorad Trbic, ordered the witness to pick up Drago Nikolic at the forward command post at Kitovnica and bring Nikolic back to the brigade command for a meeting with Main Staff security chief Ljubisa Beara and Drina Corps security chief Vujadin Popovic. The witness saw Beara and Popovic arrive and enter the barracks. At approximately 0730 or 0800 hours, give or take an hour, the witness left Standard in his car, an Opel Rekord, picked up Nikolic at the IKM, and returned to Standard about half an hour later. Nikolic went to his office for the meeting with Beara and Popovic. The witness waited in another room, and when Nikolic came out of the meeting, about 15 or 20 minutes later, he was somber and angry because he was not consulted beforehand and was ordered to find accommodation for the prisoners. Nikolic told him that there would be some people coming in for exchange. Nikolic told the witness that the witness was supposed to drive Nikolic to the Vidikovac hotel because Nikolic had been ordered to go there to wait for the buses. At approximately 0800 or 0900 hours, give or take an hour, they drove to the Vidikovac hotel and about five minutes after arriving a convoy of five or ten buses arrived carrying Muslim men guarded by civilian policemen in blue uniforms from an unknown unit. Nikolic told the witness to board the first bus and go to Orahovac and Nikolic took the car and told the witness that he would do some errands. The bus stopped at the primary school in Orahovac. The prisoners were taken from the buses into the school gymnasium by the policemen on the buses. The prisoners left their belongings in a part of the courtyard. There were no prisoners at the school when he arrived. Zvornik Brigade military police arrived approximately 20 to 30 minutes later including Trbic, Cedo Jovic, Goran Bogdanovic, a female MP named Nada, the witness's cousin, Stanoje Bircakovic, and the commander of the military police company, Miomir Jasikovac. The MPs provided security around the school. There were also a lot of curious local population there. About half an hour after the prisoners arrived, the witness saw Vujadin Popovic at the school with two of Popovic's men. At approximately 1100 hours, just after the prisoners had been taken into the gym, Drago Nikolic arrived at the school in the Opel Rekord, gave the witness the car keys, then spoke to Jasikovac and other people. Nikolic stayed for approximately an hour then departed, but left the Opel at the school. During this time, the witness was standing in front of the school which he never entered. Small TAM trucks then arrived at the school and backed up to the door. Prisoners with their hands tied were loaded on to the trucks which drove away, each with approximately 20 to 30 prisoners. Later, prisoners boarding the trucks were also blindfolded. After two or three trips, an hour or so, the witness was ordered to the best of his memory by Jasikovac to follow the trucks to a water source then return to the school. The witness did this four or five times following the trucks in the Opel. From the water source, the trucks continued on. In the evening, just before nightfall, Nikolic returned to the school, stayed for about half an hour to an hour, then told the witness to go to the IKM with him to retrieve some personal belongings. At that time, there were no more executions going on. When they passed the water source on the way, it was already dark, and in the Opel's headlights about 150 metres from the water source, they saw approximately 50 corpses on the left side of the road, about five metres from the road. They saw the same thing on the way back to Standard barracks. There was no one around the bodies and no activity. When they arrived at Standard Nikolic went to his office and the witness went home. Before they had left the school, when it was already dark, a ULT earth moving machine arrived in front of the school, stopped for five or ten minutes, then left in the direction of the trucks had been going. The next day, the witness drove Jasikovac to inspect the battalion in Pilica. On the way back they stopped for half an hour at the school in Pilica where prisoners were being held and guarded. The witness stayed on the road while Jasikovac spoke to people outside the school. So he does not know who the guards were or to whom Jasikovac spoke. The witness saw one body outside the school. They also stopped that day at the school in Rocevic where there were also prisoners guarded by members he supposed of the Zvornik Brigade. Approximately a month or two after the Orahovac executions, the witness drove Trbic to the Petkovci dam where Trbic inspected the site while the witness stayed in the car. They also travelled to Orahovac to do the same. During his testimony, the witness marked features on two photographs, that's 65 ter 3388 and 65 ter 3389. Sorry I don't have the P numbers at my fingertips. I know we just read them out but that would be P1750 and P1749 respectively. Then he corrected the markings made on those two exhibits on a third and fourth photograph, which are now P1751 and P1752. The witness also identified his entries on a travel log, which is 1748. The entries for the 14th, 15th, and 16th of July reflect locations he went to those days, but the logs do not reflect his trips to the IKM with Drago Nikolic. The logs were often filled out days after the trips were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you just a couple of follow-up questions about some of these matters that you testified about in the Popovic case. The first has to do with your escorting humanitarian aid convoys to the Yellow Bridge, Zuti Most check-point, in Bratunac. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber where, in your experience, those convoys were searched?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: The convoys were searched approximately at the bridge leading from Serbia to Bosnia and Herzegovina, which means in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by whom were they searched, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, certain people will do that, those humanitarian convoys would come rather frequently. So certain people were assigned the task to check whether the convoy really carried what was contained in its manifest, and they were also supposed to check that some other things were not present in the convoy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to which unit did those people checking those convoys belong, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: They were from the company of the military police of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly can you describe for the Trial Chamber what your personal duties were with respect to these convoys?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: My duty was to do something after the convoy had been checked. There were the Russian convoys, they transported the humanitarian aid and then I would go in front of those trucks, in rather official capacity, I would lead them along the road that went along Drina all the way to Bratunac and then from Bratunac to the Zuti Most Yellow Bridge, which is one or two kilometres from Bratunac, and I think that the Bratunac brigade had a check-point there. There were some soldiers there manning that check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn now to some of the exhibits that you were shown during your prior testimony, in particular, some of the aerial photographs of the area that you testified some of these events occurred in. In your testimony, as we just heard in the summary, you marked two photographs and then corrected the markings on those photographs when you saw them in a slightly different version. What I want to do is just show you one of those photographs and ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter 3391 in e-court, please? I'm sorry that's [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now P1752.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 1752, absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you see an image in front of you, sir, on your computer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The -- in your prior testimony, you identified in this exhibit, if we see the long white straight line at the bottom of the picture, and you can almost see two parallel lines within that long straight line, you identified that as the railroad track, and above that we see another white line that's a little bit more curvy almost parallel to that lower line, and you identified that as the road. And you wrote down a W and made a mark indicating where the water source was, and you also drew an arrow on that smaller road that turns off the main road that leads underneath the railroad track and you marked that with a T during your testimony for "truck." Do you remember making all those markings in the Popovic trial, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. When we met on Sunday and I showed you a copy of this exhibit, you made some other markings, and I want to just show them to the Trial Chamber and ask you to explain them. And if we could have the assistance of court officer, I think it would be better to put this one on the ELMO, but in the meantime let's put it up on e-court and see how legible it is, but I think it's going to -- and this is 7166, I'm not sure it's going to be at legible as we'd like. And if I could just have the original handed to the witness so he can look at it as well. I think that's pretty good on e-court so we won't need the ELMO, but I would like to show this original. Sir, we can see on the screen the same image that we just saw except that there is a little red circle with an X through it on the opposite side of that smaller road that you marked with the arrow. Can you just explain to the Trial Chamber what your red mark there denotes? Explain why you put that on there during our proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: When we were looking at the same shot the last time, it was aligned in a different way so the water spring cannot be seen from the direction of Orahovac but from the direction of Krizevici, and it's on the other side, so I assume that the last time the photo was turned. And that's why you could see it in a different way from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So where you've marked that circle with the X, what exactly does that indicate? Just so you can explain it to the Trial Chamber. What does that circle with the X show?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: This shows the water spring, the fountain, which is across the road. I came to this point on several occasions when I went with the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you encountered or when you saw that water point when you were following the trucks, where did the trucks go after the water point?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: They went to the left along the road towards the railway tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And again, have you indicated that on this sketch with anything?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is an arrow pointing in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P1753, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to ask you some questions about another exhibit you were shown, and this is P1748. And again with some assistance, I would just hand the originals to the witness. They will be pretty legible on e-court. They are just in sequential order so -- and the Defence will see it, and I think also, if the Trial Chamber wishes to see these exhibits, they are discussed at some length in the witness's testimony and they are much more legible in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Principal reasons, the Chamber would like to see them as well. In the meantime, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see -- and can we have the -- great -- B/C/S, the original up there. Do you see the document on the screen? And if you do, could you just tell the Trial Chamber what it is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a travel order, a vehicle work log, that was used in order to be able to record the movement of the vehicle at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And in your Popovic testimony, you testified that this exhibit actually incorporates three separate travel logs for that same vehicle, the Opel Rekord. They were just filled out on different occasions. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber has had the opportunity to look at these -- the original documents. They may be given back to the Prosecution, I think, or to the witness, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And once the witness has discussed a particular page, Mr. President, I may invite the Trial Chamber again to take a look at that particular page. Now, if we can go to page 3 in the English and that will also be page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And sir, if you can go to the second document, I believe, in -- out of those three that you have there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could have also the B/C/S on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, we see here a vehicle work log for an Opel Rekord with your name listed as the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would just turn the page over, sir, and take a look at the opposite side of the page, you testified about the locations you drove various people to on the 14th, 15th, and 16th, including Drago Nikolic and Jasikovac. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber just briefly what information is in column 4? And we are looking at the dates for the 14th, 15th, and 16th. What does column 4 show us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: That column shows the movement of the vehicles, the route.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at all the way at column 20, we see a column of signatures. Can you identify whose signatures those are in that column?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the first signature on top is Drago Nikolic's, and I believe the last two are Trbic's signature but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in between? In between the first one and the last two, whose signatures are those?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And again, Your Honours, because it's not so legible on e-court, if you'd like to look at the original of this particular log, which was discussed at some length, I'd invite the Trial Chamber to do so. Otherwise, we'll have it available any time the Chamber wishes to review it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think at the moment there is no need for that, but perhaps you can ask the witness to read out what is written in column 4 to have a full understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Bircakovic, you've heard the request of the Trial Chamber. If you would, please read out the route for the dates of the 14th of July and the two entries for the 15th of July and the entry for the 16th of July, please. If you just start with the route that you've written in for the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did we show this in printed form if the witness is supposed to read it out of the original list? Because we see now in print form the same words as in handwriting, so there is no need for him in that case to read the handwritten form, and that is inappropriate if we are trying to adduce evidence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there is no problem, Mr. Tolimir. When I made my request, at that moment we didn't have the English translation on the left-hand side of the screen. I think we can see it now that there are all these routes written also in the English and therefore it's not necessary to read it out. I didn't know that we had this English translation available. Please continue, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness, we are done with these documents for now. Just a couple of additional questions. You testified in the Popovic trial that you recalled seeing Beara and Popovic at the Standard command in Karakaj in the morning of 14 July. Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you remember exactly when it was that you saw them that morning or is your memory unclear about precisely when you saw them that morning?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall the exact hour, whether it was 8.00 or 8.30 or 9.00. So I'm not exactly sure about the exact hour because nobody really paid any attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you've told us in the past that they were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were they wearing anything on their heads that you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: They had the sort of caps normally worn by officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your recollection, were they wearing anything else that would have indicated who they were, in particular, to you other than just the fact that you, as you had testified, had seen them around before?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew Popovic much better than I did Beara, because I used to see them around before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. For my last question, I want to turn your attention to a document which you were shown during your OTP interview in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And for the Defence, that was at pages 108 to 112 in the English, 111 to 115 in the B/C/S. If we could have 65 ter 340 on e-court. I apologise, Your Honours, I neglected to put this on the list of exhibits. It has a 65 ter number but that somehow didn't make it on our list of proposed exhibits. It has never been used with the witness in court before and it has been -- it was shown to numerous witnesses in the prior trial, but I notice that he was shown it in his interview and I apologise, I simply forgot to put this on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, I can state that my remark that this was the last we saw, but we are not sure if this will be the last one, that there was a foundation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To quote one of America's finest men of letters, Yogi Berra: "It ain't over till it's over." If we could have page 2 of the English on e-court, please? And if we could go a couple more pages, I think it's going to be page 3 in the original. And with the court officer's assistance, I'd like to hand the original to the witness. And just to let the Trial Chamber know, I did show this to the witness in proofing, and it was included in the proofing note which went over to the Defence so at least they have been on notice about its use, if not the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you see a document in front of you, both on the screen and that you're reading?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a list of the personnel of the military police company of the Zvornik Brigade, and we can see that it shows what their assignments were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in short, it indicates whether they were absent, present, or at a particular location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to save a little bit of time we can see at numbers 1, 4, 5, and 7, the names of some of the MPs who you described during your testimony seeing at the school in Orahovac: Jasikovac, the MP named Nada, Goran Bogdanovic, and Cedo Jovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could Mr. Thayer tell us whether this document was produced on the spot where these people were or whether it was produced in the offices, on the premises of the unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think Mr. Thayer is examining the witness at the moment. He may follow this suggestion or not, but you are entitled to put this question to the witness during your cross-examination. Mr. Thayer, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just to save a little bit of time, if we keep turning the pages, I think we can all agree that we'll see the name of your cousin Stanoje Bircakovic and, in fact, your own name on this -- on this roster; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your interview with the OTP, you told the investigator who you believed was in charge of maintaining this roster. Can you tell the Trial Chamber who that person was, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that it was maintained by Stevo Kostic. He was the company clerk, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in July of 1995 did you personally actually see this roster?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bircakovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer. Now Mr. Tolimir is commencing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please retain this document in e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I forgot to ask Mr. Thayer and Mr. Thayer forgot to tender this document, I think. Is that not your --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Indeed I forgot, Mr. President. We would tender 65 ter 340, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P1754. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And my apologies for interrupting you, Mr. Tolimir. Now the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May peace reign in this house and I hope that -- may God's will be done in these proceedings and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish. Now, could we just keep this document that we've just seen a moment ago because I would like to put some questions in relation to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, good morning and please try and answer my question. A moment ago, when Mr. Thayer asked you about this document, he asked you whether this document showed who was actually present at the site in question. And that is why I wanted to ask whether Mr. Thayer could check with you whether this document was actually produced on the site or some place else. Could you tell us that, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Bircakovic, did you understand the question of Mr. Tolimir? It was a question put to you. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. But I thought the question was meant for someone else. Well, I'm not sure where it was produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: All the questions are put to you as a witness, and now Mr. Tolimir is examining you. Please answer the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know where it was produced or when. This is the first time that I actually see this document and I never had occasion earlier to do so. I know that when we were given assignments, there was a notebook, an A4 format notebook, where notes were made. I've never seen a log of this type.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this graph with names, does it show where these individuals were or does it show information about the attendance of these men within the unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, again, I don't really know. Most probably this shows the deployment of those men, but I'm not really sure whether that is absolutely accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now please see the entire roster on the screen for the witness to see it because he said that this was a list of deployments. So I would like the witness to check, see what it says there, and tell us whether all these individuals were on one and the same site at the same time or not.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, people were in different areas. There were a lot of men in the company. So they were in different locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For instance, if we take a look at the first line there, at the end, in the columns 21 -- 20, 21, and 22, it says, SL for these three individuals. Do you know what this SL actually indicates?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I don't. I don't know what those letters denote.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, below that, you see some pluses and then in the next column we again see SL, SL, and then below that we see where it says, in the same columns, BO, BO, BO. Do you know what the BO denotes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see below that, where it says, "Killed," for instance, for Mr. Mico Mitar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on this, can you tell us whether these individuals were on the same location at the same time or whether this just shows whether they were with the unit or on the premises because it's very important for the transcript to clarify whether they were all in the same place or not.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, here it says that this person was killed. In other words, he was dead. The man was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this is the first time that you see this list and you cannot really comment on it and what it denotes, would you agree that this document be admitted into evidence through you or whether it should actually be done through a commander within this brigade or some other person, the person who kept the log maybe?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It's not really up to me, and I don't know whether this document can or cannot be admitted. That's not my business.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Now, tell us again, were any of these individuals with you at the time when you drove Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was any of these individuals from the roster with you at the time when you saw in the barracks as it says here Popovic and Beara together?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure there was someone there but I can't really recall. There were other colleagues, there were some people at the gate, and at the entrance, but I don't really recall or I don't really know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see -- can we conclude based on this paper, what the assignments were? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. I'm not familiar with this. I don't know whether it shows that or not. I don't know what these letters denote.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please see if you can find your name on this list? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't see it on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Perhaps we can see the previous page, the beginning of this roster or maybe at the end. Maybe because your last name begins with a B, maybe it's at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to save some time, Mr. President, it will be page 4 in English, it's the second-to-the-last page in the original, it's number 85.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have it on the screen, number 85. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Bircakovic, can you tell us whether one can read on the roster what your tasks were on the days marked on the list?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the letters stand for. I don't know what this person who kept the record had in mind when writing these letters. I can see letter O, letter P.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bircakovic. Can you tell us what it was that you were doing on any of the dates? You take a pick. Be it the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, but what it was that you were doing based on the markings made here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my duty was, at the beginning of the day, if I didn't have to take Drago Popovic [as interpreted], or any of the -- or if I didn't have to take him personally anywhere, I would take any of the other senior officers. I would drive them wherever I was required and that was the case for any of these days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I had to put this question to you. You weren't the recording clerk but it was stated here that you were all at the same location, and hence it would transpire that you all took part in these relevant events at this time. Thank you. This is my next question. Based on what you just said, that whenever you needed to drive Drago Nikolic you would do so or else you would be at anybody else's disposal, does this mean that you were Drago Nikolic's personal driver or what was your duty exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, initially, 98 per cent of my work was for Drago Nikolic. Later on, there was something that transpired between Drago Nikolic and Pandurevic, who somewhat restricted his right to the vehicle so the vehicle was placed at the disposal of the command. From there on, I would drive anybody who needed the vehicle, including Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said initially but can you please set a time-frame? For the Court's purposes we need to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say it was as of 1994 that I would take Drago wherever he needed to go, but I would also take Obrenovic or Pandurevic to Zvornik if they didn't have their vehicles available.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During cross-examination, on page 9, line 8, you were asked if you escorted convoys going from the Serbian border towards Srebrenica. If you recall, Mr. Thayer asked you first where it was checked, you said it was at Karakaj, and then you escorted to the yellow bridge; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what exactly were your duties as you escorted these vehicles to the Yellow Bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on how many trucks there were, three, four, five, while I was escorting them I was at the head of the column. We would go from Drinjaca across Zelinje to Bratunac and on to the Yellow Bridge. We had our own check-point, that's to say the VRS, the Bratunac Brigade, at the Yellow Bridge. The convoy would proceed past our check-point and some 200 metres further down there was a UN check-point, so they would go all the way there, unload the humanitarian aid, I would wait for the trucks to return, and then escort them to Karakaj from where they proceeded on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If anybody wanted to stop them on the stretch of the road from your point of departure to the Yellow Bridge, would you have to do anything?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's why we were there but we didn't have any such instances of anybody stopping the convoy, people were aware that the convoy had to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If anybody wanted to do anything to the convoy in terms of tampering with it or putting anything into it, would you have prevented this from happening?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course we would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to your statement now. This is a statement you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal. My legal adviser will give me the reference number now. It's 6674.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we have page 1 shown in e-court so that the witness has the document before him, since I'm going to be putting questions about it? Thank you. We have page 1 on our screens. In line 12 from the top, you are told that you were summoned for this interview as an indicted person; am I right? Firstly, I would like to confirm the fact that you were summonsed here as an indictee; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not right. Not as an indictee but as a suspect initially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure what General Tolimir is reading from but clearly the witness understood either from his memory or from reading it himself in his own language what the proper status of the witness was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I want to let Mr. Thayer know that I'm reading from the document which has the text contained in the table. So can this error be corrected, please? Because the witness was there as a suspect, not as an indictee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have it now clear on the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now try and recall the beginning of the interview and answer the following question:

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you at the outset told what the events were going to be that they were going to ask you about? And I mean, did the investigators tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. They only announced that they would be asking me about these events.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 3 shown? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can read through quickly, if you want to. These are questions put to you by investigator Manning and your answers. I'd just like to briefly go through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can the document that we have on our right-hand side be removed? Because the one on the left-hand side contains both the Serbian and English text. There is no need to complicate things in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is really a very good proposal. Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In line 4, Mr. Manning -- or rather, in line 6 from the top, Mr. Manning tells you: "At the conclusion of record of interview, I will give you the opportunity to ask me questions clarifying certain things. I will also arrange for a copy of the tape to be sent to you. Do you have any questions about what I have just explained to you?" And you say that you don't. And then he goes on to tell you what will transpire. He introduces himself. And then in the last line on this page, he says: "We are investigating what happened to a large number of men after the fall of Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to the next page, page 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: He goes on to say: "... who were captured or surrendered to the VRS forces and were subsequently executed by the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska, including the Drina Corps and the Zvornik Brigade. "So do you understand what it is that we are investigating and which questions I'm going to put to you?" And then further down, you answer in the affirmative. So this is my question: Based on this, does it follow that Mr. Manning first told you what the events were that he was going to ask you about and then proceeded to put questions to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it does follow from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will not be asking you about what it is that you were doing in the period leading up to 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I want you to see it and then I'll put several questions to you based on your answers contained on that page. Thank you. In line 18, the Prosecutor asked you who the superior to Jasikovac was. And then in line 19, you said that it was Drago Nikolic. And then in line 21, that he was subordinated to the brigade commander. Since there are several things that need clarifying for the sake of the transcripts, can you tell us who was the commanding officer to Mr. Jasikovac?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Jasikovac was subordinated to Drago Nikolic. Vinko Pandurevic was the brigade commander. Whatever order he gave to Drago, he could equally have given to Jasikovac, even if he didn't give one to Drago, be it in Drago's presence or absence, whenever Jasikovac was there in the compound of the barracks, he could have given an order to him or to Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You're a soldier, you know that there is the principle of singleness of command. And you enter and there is also the principle of duality of command, singleness of command means that you only can have one commanding officer giving you orders, in the other case you would have two. So my question is: Could Drago Nikolic have issued orders to Jasikovac without Vinko Pandurevic being aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think that it was at the meetings that Pandurevic would give orders to Nikolic who in turn would convey them to Jasikovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know if there were times when Jasikovac would receive orders directly from Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: With this in mind, did Drago have, as part of his powers, the power to command the military police company of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what sort of relationship they had. What I do know is that he would receive orders both from Vinko Pandurevic and Drago. What sort of an arrangement they had, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the term "command" stands for?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know what we were receiving was called daily commands. Now, what it means --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was a military police company given daily commands by Pandurevic or Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not 100 per cent sure. Our company clerk would have a roster, and every morning when we had a lineup, he had a paper containing daily commands detailing assignments for the day, whether they concerned work out in the field or something else. He would be best placed to tell you who gave him these daily orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what sort of duties Drago Nikolic had as the security officer of the brigade? Did he have the power to issue orders to units other than military police units? Tell us if you know.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure. I don't think it would be useful to say anything on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know if he was only entitled to carry out the measures and actions as ordered by the commander, or was he also entitled to carry these out independently of his own accord?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, based on the activities carried out at the time, it would seem to me that he wasn't really entitled to make independent decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will look at item 122 of the rules governing these issues, we will have them -- we will have that item shown on our screens. It is the rules of the infantry, motorised, mountain, light brigades that was used by the JNA and subsequently by the VRS until the arrival of NATO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is 1D565. In English it's page 38 and in Serbian page 66. Thank you. I'll say it once again. It's 1D565, page 38 in Serbian and page 66 in English. Maybe it's not in e-court. I was just told that it isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Gajic, you should check it again because the registrar is not able to find it in e-court. Now it's working.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you to the staff handling the e-court. We apologise that we haven't prepared everything in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to read one sentence from Rule 122. We are now talking about the soldier, not an officer, and the witness was the driver of the brigade officers. So now, when you take a look at the Rule 122, I'm going to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President I just ask that we wait until we actually have the relevant page, and I don't know if there is a Defence list of cross-examination exhibits. We haven't got one. I understand sometimes these things happen, but don't know if it's a big list or a little list and it would just be helpful to know what's coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, the Chamber didn't receive such a list. Now we have paragraph 122 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was just told by my legal adviser that he prepared everything for the next witness for today and that it is true that Mr. Thayer had not been informed beforehand that we were going to use the same documents with this witness as well. So now we can read it here both in English and Serbian. It's point 122 and that's the only thing I'm going to be reading out from this document. I quote, 122: "The security organ is a specialised organ of the command which organises and implements measures and procedures of counter-intelligence support. It also participates in recommending, organising, and implementing security and self-protection measures which concern the command and other subjects of self-protection." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So my question is as follows: Is this in accordance with what you said earlier, that he can only implement the things that had been ordered beforehand by the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, more or less yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So did that happen in practice? You spent a lot of time with him. You drove him and other officers very often. So did that happen in practice?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly how things went on in practice, how they did those things. I'm not sure. I'm not sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 13, line 3 of today's transcript, during your direct examination -- I'm sorry, I lost my note. Maybe you remember. The question posed to you, went as follows: When you drove Drago on Trbic's orders and when he saw Beara and Popovic for the first time, was he angry because he had not been informed beforehand that the prisoners would have been deployed in his zone? Do you remember that part?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So based on that, do you know anything about -- could you say anything about whether Drago said it sincerely or he only acted up in front of you and he knew what it was all about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he acted up or not. He was in bad mood. He came out pretty angry. And you could see that he was in bad mood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you said that he was angry and that he didn't know about the deployment of the prisoners. That's what you said answering the first question by Mr. Thayer. And after that, you said that you entered the bus and he took the car. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then did you see Beara and Popovic when he came back in about 20 minutes? Because you said that he came back with them.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw them at the beginning, in the morning, and then after that, when he came out, we simply went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see them immediately before Drago Nikolic met them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, in the morning. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Then why did you go to fetch Drago? Could you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because Trbic told me to go and pick up Drago, because Popovic and Beara arrived and a meeting was supposed to be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, does that mean that Nikolic did not know that they had arrived and that he was supposed to have a meeting with them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us go back to page 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is it possible to deal with that next part of this document after the break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, we must have our first break now and we will resume after half an hour, at 11.00, and the court usher will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have now in e-court 6674? That's a statement by this witness. And I would like to have page 15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this is page 15, eighth row, eighth row, and 27th from the other side. You were asked by the investigator about who gave you the tasks. And then you say: "We were not given any direct orders. We received our orders through the company commander." You can see now that the cursor now is in that part. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Now, was it exclusively the company commander who issued you orders or was it sometimes also somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the company commander who then in turn received orders from other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you and Drago Nikolic know that those prisoners were to be brought into your brigade and that would you have to find accommodation for them? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did Drago know that they were to come to the brigade or did he only find that out at the meeting to which you took him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think he found out at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But from whom did he learn that they arrived into the zone of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But did you say that Trbic had sent you to drive him to the brigade because some officers had arrived to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that he knew that, because he did have some sort of link with the brigade. When I arrived, he was already waiting for me outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, Trbic may have informed him about that but did you know that the prisoners would be put up in those schools, the Muslims captured in Srebrenica and Zepa? Did you know that before you went to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not go to the meeting and I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Excuse me, I mentioned Zepa in the transcript it was my mistake. It should have been Srebrenica. Thank you. And thank you to Aleksandar. Did you receive orders from the commander of the military police company or did you receive orders from somebody else in those cases when you were about to drive people who were not from military police?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I would receive orders from others as well. I had very little contact with the company commander. I was a driver, which means that the duty operative would schedule the tasks for vehicles and they would give me my orders about where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So would it be right to conclude that you, as a driver, received orders more frequently from the traffic service or from the person who was in charge of assigning vehicles to different tasks than from Jasikovac?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I would receive it from the traffic service, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that the brigade commander took away the right from Drago Nikolic to have a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't entirely cancel this entitlement to a vehicle. It is simply that when he had nowhere -- no tasks, he didn't have to go anywhere, then that vehicle would have been given at the disposal of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what you stated in your statement, page 17, line 3. You said that you were also assigned to drive others. Now, can we take a look at page 18? It's line 31 to 42. It's at the bottom. The nine lines at the bottom, that's what I want to ask you about. My question is as follows: Did the investigator, Dean Manning, while he was interrogating you, would he first tell you what he knew about the events in Srebrenica in 1995 and then ask you to confirm this information, or did he ask you what you yourself knew about this execution of several thousand people?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one and the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I'll quote what he said in line 31, page 18. He said: "I said I was going to ask you questions about execution of thousands of Muslim men from Srebrenica. Do you agree that that happened?" That's what he asked you. And then you said: "I do agree but I don't know to which extent." To which he said: "What do you mean by that? The numbers?" And then you said: "Yes, the numbers." And then he said: "I'm going to ask you about questions about killings, about organisation for killings many thousands of men." That's what he says in page -- in line 41. Also based on this we can see that he would first put something to you and then he would just ask you about it. Is that how it actually happened?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, for a part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Did the investigator, Mr. Manning, first put to you whatever the evidence that he had and then ask you to tell him about what you knew about it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. He would say things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at this page, 19, line 3 from the top, where Mr. Dean Manning says the following: "We have eye witnesses of the killings. We have survivors who are part of execution who were shot at. We have aerial images of the executions taking place. We have seized records from the Zvornik Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade, and we have many people those brigades in the Drina Corps interviewed. We have your documents as well from the military police and from the daily assignments. What I would like you to understand is that it's very important for you to tell the truth." Thank you. Now, does this suggest that he would first put things to you and then only ask you to comment or answer his questions about the things that he had put to you earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the investigator in the course of the interview tell you that he had taken part in the exhumations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think he did mention it on one occasion. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at page 19, then, lines 27, 28, 30, 31 through 35, where he says the following: "If you try to hide what happened or hide your part in what happened, your knowledge of what happened, I can prove that you are lying, and I want you to understand that this is your chance to tell the truth here and now. I have personally exhumed bodies of thousands and thousands of men and boys," and then he says, "from Kozluk, from Branjevo, the military farm, from the dam above the factory in Karakaj, from Pilica, from the Kravica warehouse, from Orahovac." And then next page, please, page 20: "And as I said, I want to ask you questions about that." Does this actually show that he would first put things that he knew about to you and then ask you to comment on it or say what you know about it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, sort of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see that as some kind of pressure that he was putting on you where he wanted you to confirm what he was saying because he said at one point, "I can prove to you that you're lying," so isn't that a form of pressure? He said to you that you were lying, that he can say that to you, before you even said anything.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, maybe you could say it was a form of pressure, but it wasn't really pressure. I couldn't say things about something that I didn't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at page 20 now. On page 20, in the last line, you say: "Drago Nikolic told me that some people were supposed to be brought in for exchange, I don't know what exactly and how, and that he had been ordered that simply these men were sent to him." And then on the next page: "He wasn't asked about it, they were just sent over to him. He didn't know anything about it. At the beginning he was very angry when he came out of the meeting, that was at the military command," and so on and so forth. So my question is this: From what you've said here to Dean Manning, can we conclude that Drago Nikolic didn't know and that you didn't know that these men would be brought to your area, the man that you later met at Vidikovac?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well he didn't know until he was told about it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now please see page 26 of your statement? On page 26 in lines 35 through 42, so that's the last five lines on the page, Mr. Dean Manning asks you the following: "Was Beara at the school on the 14th?" And you say: "I don't think so but I'm not sure." And then he says -- and then you say: "As for Popovic, I'm not sure I remember like through the fog that he might have been. But I'm not 100 per cent sure. Maybe. But I can't really say because," now the next page, please, "because this was a long time ago, these times are long over. Sometimes I don't even know what's happened today," and so on and so forth. So my question is: Did you make it very clear, did you say it very clearly to the Prosecutor, that you can't say anything about things that you can't recall?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. You could say -- you could put it that way. As for Beara, he was certainly not there, and as for Popovic, yeah, well, he was and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Prosecutor expect you to confirm that you had seen Beara at the school in Orahovac on the 14th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, he didn't insist on that. He just put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please take a look at page 27, line 11, where you state the following. But before that, let's take a look at line 6 where you say -- what he says to you actually: "You must remember this, you remember this very well, don't you?" That's what the Prosecutor asked you. And then he says in the next line: "But you don't want to remember it." And you say: "Well, no. Let me tell you, I can't say what I don't remember. What I did see I'm not denying. I can't say that I was not in Orahovac on that day because I was, and I can't say that I did not bring in Drago. My duty was to drive the car," and so on and so forth. So my question is this: As the driver, did you, of necessity, have to know about the tasks and the things that the people you drove did and their assignments and their missions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's take a look at line 26, that's the fourth line from the bottom. Or rather the 7th line, where he says to you: "I also understand that you don't want to tell me who was at the killing point in Orahovac." And then he says to you: "I need you to tell me that." And then you say: "Well, I cannot tell you something that I did not see. Because you see I can't say that you were there and killing people if I haven't -- if I didn't see you." And then on the next page, 28, can we see it, please, lines 1, 2, and 3: "This is -- these are very serious charges, it's not like saying that somebody has broken into a car and stolen something, you see." So these are your words. "I cannot say things that I haven't seen them -- that I haven't seen." Thank you. So my question is: During the interview, were there several attempts to actually draw some answers from you based on the knowledge that the investigators had from their previous interviews with the participants in the events?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they weren't really trying to force the answers out of me or extort them out of me. I was just telling them about what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that you told them about what you had seen and what knowledge you had, but did they believe you? Because they are almost putting it to you that you were the organiser of sorts, so how could a simple soldier be in charge of organising something, events that were some 100 kilometres away, further away? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the general has really crossed the line at this point. We've had many, many questions about the conduct of this interview, the witness has remained consistent in his answers. I don't need to characterise them for the Trial Chamber. Now we have another characterisation of the alleged behaviour of the investigator, Mr. Manning, and if the general is going to make a statement which so far has been completely unsupported, he should just read the interview where Mr. Manning says: "That's why I said at your level you are not held responsible for the plan." It's this kind of mischaracterisation which is not helpful for the Trial Chamber and it's misleading to the witness if he's going to make these kinds of characterisations without any support, in fact, in direct contravention of the very words of the transcript that he is selectively choosing from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are reading from the record of the interview of -- by Mr. Manning and you got several answers about the role of the witness. You should focus on his position and put questions in relation to his possible knowledge, and referring to your last question, of course, the question itself is okay: "How could a simple soldier be in charge of organising something, events that were some 100 kilometres away, further away?" If you think this question is really helpful to clarify the situation, then put the question to the witness, but focus, please, on his position and his duties as a driver, as he explained several times. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I put that question because we are in a courtroom and you have cautioned the witness of his status of a suspect, and I put the question to him, and he can answer either with a "yes" or "no," and I asked him whether he could be held responsible for something that was -- that had happened in Srebrenica, and he said he was clear in his answer. Now, my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you put a different question to him, not about his responsibility but about the -- if he was in charge of organising something. It's quite different. Just continue your questioning. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, let's hear from the witness whether he could have had anything to do with any organising of anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should put the question in a different way. Were you in the position and did you organise something like that Mr. Tolimir is referring to? Did you organise something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. How could I have? I was just a driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, sir, can you please tell us this? Did your commanders and your superiors ever instruct you that you should actually hide things that you did during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness. I will not dwell on other issues such as the manner the interview was conducted. I would like to thank you, witness, for coming to testify and thank you for answering my questions and I wish you a safe trip home and may God bless you. Mr. Presiding Judge, my cross-examination of this witness is complete and I have no further questions for him. Thank you. I would just like to tender this into evidence, this statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are referring to the interview of the witness by the OTP, you have quoted from, 65 ter 6674; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. It's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D147, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have used another document, at least one paragraph of the rules of the brigade from 1984, 1D565. Is it necessary to tender these rules? Perhaps you will use them with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It can be admitted. I will be using it with the next witness because that's who it was intended for to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Does that have a translation, the full text?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The entire rules have been translated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D148, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I do have a brief re-examination just on one issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have D147 on e-court, please? Actually, we're here. If we could go to page 112 - and we can get rid of the English - 112 of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, you were shown a copy of the military police roster for July of 1995. In fact, you were shown the original that you had in your hand and the copy was on the computer. Do you recall being asked about that military police roster during your interview with Mr. Manning in 2002?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall being shown a copy of that roster during your interview in 2002?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So when you told us today that this was the first time that you had seen this document, did you mean that it was the first time you saw the original or did you just forget that you had been shown it or if you could just explain to the Trial Chamber your answer to those questions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had not been shown the document in a courtroom before. This was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go back just two pages, please. And if we could just scroll all the way down to the bottom of the document, we can see that here, Mr. Manning says he has another document he wants to show you, and he reads out the ERN which I think everyone will agree is the same ERN on this document. If we could go to the next page, he asks you: "Now, if you can look at that document, tell me what it is." And you say: "It's a list of the company of the military police," and then you identify a number of names who you recall of MPs who were with you or who you saw at Orahovac on the 14th of July. Do you recall these questions during your interview, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then you were asked, towards the bottom of this page, if you look down towards the bottom: "Tell me how this document is created?" And you ask him: "Well, what do you mean created?" And manning asked you: "Who makes the document?" And you answered: "I think it's the responsibility of the company record keeper." And if we go to the next page, you identify that person as Stevo Kostic. My first question is: Do you recall these questions and your answers and if you do, do you stand by them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you testified today, at page 29, in answer to a question from General Tolimir, that: "Our company clerk would have a roster and every morning, when we had a lineup, he had a paper containing daily commands detailing assignments for the day, whether they concerned work out in the field or something else. He would be best placed to tell you who gave him these daily orders." Now, again, this company clerk that you referred to in your answer to General Tolimir's question, what is that person's name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: That was Stevo Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So it's the same person we are talking about. Now --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Manning asks you what a number of the letters that appear on this log mean. He shows you where there are Ts and where there are Ps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could look at P1754, please, and if we could go to the last page in the B/C/S first, and just rotate that, and the last page in the English as well, sorry for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We see the letter T and it says "terrain" or "teren." What does that mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: It means that the individual was out in the field, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we see a number of abbreviations here and it's sort of a key. Do you know who wrote this? Can you recognise the handwriting or do you know who wrote this key at the end of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Stevo Kostic who wrote this, though I don't recall his handwriting. I just assume it's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say you assume it's him, can you tell the Trial Chamber why you assume that it's Stevo Kostic who is writing down this key at the back of this roster?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because he was charged with these daily assignments, and I can't confirm that he wrote it because I'm not familiar with his handwriting. He would normally write those assignments for the day, so I assume that he wrote the key as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go back to D147 for just a quick minute, please. And if we just focus on the B/C/S version, the one that has both the English and the B/C/S, and go to -- let's start with page 114, okay. And if we could go back one page, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In brief, we can see that Mr. Manning put to you that the entries or some of the entries on this original roster had been erased, that there had been an O on the log, on the roster, for certain people on the 14th of July, and that that O had been erased and been replaced with a T, which we saw from the legend or from the key stands for "terrain."
